events.text: Day 1 begins.

Kenji here. We have no information yet, so I want to start by collecting observations rather than accusing anyone. I'm a villager and I'm not claiming any special role. Amara, you opened the game, so I'd like your read on the table. Did anyone's opening remarks or early behavior stand out to you, even slightly? Please be specific about what you noticed, so we can compare notes without guessing.

Thanks for the question, Kenji — I'll answer it directly. Honestly, with only one message on the table, there's very little behavior to read. But two things do stand out to me. First, you opened by declaring 'I'm a villager and I'm not claiming any special role' before anyone accused you of anything. That's an unprompted soft claim on Day 1. It's not damning — plenty of honest players do it to set a cooperative tone — but it's worth noting that mafia also use exactly that phrasing to buy goodwill early. I'd file it as a weak signal, nothing more. Second, your question to me was well-formed and process-oriented, which reads slightly more town than mafia to my eye, since a mafia opener often prefers vaguer 'let's not accuse anyone' framing without giving anyone anything to respond to. You did that framing AND asked a substantive question, so I'm leaning neutral-positive on you for now, with the caveat that one message is a tiny sample. Beyond that, my actual read on the table is this: nobody has tripped anything yet, and I don't want to manufacture suspicion out of thin air on Day 1 — fake reads invented from nothing are how mafia set up mislynches. What I'd rather do is build a record we can compare against once we have a night result. So here's what I'm watching for as the day goes on: who avoids committing to any read at all, who piles onto the first target without their own reasoning, and who pushes 'no lynch today' energy hardest — that last one is a classic mafia comfort position when they're unsure of the vote math. I'll also say plainly that I have no power role, same as you — no investigation, no protection, nothing. I'm a plain villager, and I'd rather say that once, cleanly, than dance around it. My plan today is to vote for whoever has accumulated the most genuinely suspicious behavior by vote time, and if that's nobody, I'll abstain rather than push a random elimination — but I want to hear whether others share that bar or would rather force a Day 1 lynch for information. That disagreement matters a lot for how we read each other later.

Amara, I'll respond directly to your points. One thing stands out: you flagged Kenji's unprompted villager claim as a potential mafia tell, then made the exact same kind of claim yourself two sentences later. That doesn't make you suspicious on its own, but if that behavior is genuinely a weak signal, it applies equally to both of you — and I think it's worth all of us being honest about that rather than letting one person's framing stick while the other walks it back. On your question about Day 1 voting — I lean toward your position, but with a caveat. Forcing a lynch with zero information is how town hands mafia an easy mislynch, and I'd rather abstain unless someone genuinely slips. However, a pure abstain-everything approach also benefits mafia, who can hide comfortably in a game where nobody is ever eliminated. The bar should be: vote when someone's behavior actually warrants it, not on vibes or pressure. Kenji, you're the only other voice on the table so far — where do you land on this? Would you rather see a forced Day 1 lynch for the information it produces, or hold to a higher bar like Amara and I are suggesting?

Maya, fair point, and I'll own it: Amara and I made nearly identical villager claims, so neither of us should get a free pass on that tell. I'm not treating either one as a real signal. On your question, I land between you two. I won't force a Day 1 lynch on zero information, because a random elimination just hands mafia a free town vote. But I agree that abstaining every day favors mafia, so I want a concrete threshold. For me, that means someone contradicts their own earlier statement, dodges a direct question, or pushes a vote without giving reasons. Any one of those would be enough for me to vote. Amara, you said you'd abstain rather than push a random elimination. Does that still hold if the table is split by the end of today? Maya, I'm asking you specifically: what would have to happen today for you to put a vote on someone, and would you vote on a Day 1 lean without a specific reason?

Kenji, direct answers to both of your questions.

On Amara's position — I can't speak for her, but from my side, a split table at vote time is exactly when you can't afford to abstain silently. If the table ends up split with no clear logic behind either side, someone is organizing a mislynch, and staying quiet would let that happen. I'd vote then, but only after naming my reasoning out loud first.

On what would move me to vote: you already named the thresholds I care about — contradiction, dodging a direct question, or a vote with no reasoning. I'd add one more: voting pattern. If someone's stated position today doesn't match where their vote actually lands, that's the kind of inconsistency I'd call out publicly.

Would I vote on a Day 1 lean without a specific reason? No. A lean isn't a reason. If I can't articulate why someone is suspicious in concrete terms — something they said, something they avoided — I'd abstain and say so openly. Voting without that would be exactly the kind of unexplained elimination that helps whoever's hiding.

I also want to flag something for the rest of the table: six players haven't spoken yet — Isha, Leo, Theo, Arjun, Lucia, Noah. I'm not suspicious of anyone for staying quiet this early, but I do want to hear from all of you before vote time. Silence from a large bloc is the easiest place for mafia to sit undetected. Whatever your read is — even if it's 'no read' — put it on the record so we have something to compare against later.

That's my bar going into vote time. I'm not looking to force a lynch today unless someone gives me a real reason.

Noah here. I'm one of the silent players Maya called out, so I'll put my read on record. I have no strong scum read yet. My notes so far: Kenji and Amara both made unprompted villager/no-power claims; Maya correctly flagged the symmetry, and Kenji owned it. By itself that's not a reason to vote either of them. I do want Amara to address that symmetry directly, since she framed an unprompted villager claim as a weak mafia signal before making the same kind of claim herself. If she has a reason her claim differs, I want to hear it; if not, I'll treat it as neutral for both rather than a point against Kenji. I agree with the threshold Maya and Kenji stated: no forced Day 1 lynch on zero information; vote only for a concrete contradiction, a dodge of a direct question, or a vote with no reasoning. I'll abstain if nothing meets that bar. I'd also like the other silent players to state their bar, not just 'no read,' so we have a record. Amara, specifically: do you still consider unprompted villager claims a weak mafia signal, and if so, how do you square that with your own claim? Please answer that directly.

Noah asked me to address this directly, so I will. Yes, I still consider an unprompted villager claim a weak mafia signal — weak, meaning it moves my read almost nothing on its own. I made my own claim immediately after Kenji's because I had already decided to answer his question about the table, and burying my own position while prodding his would have been exactly the asymmetry Maya flagged. I flagged the tell, then neutralized it on myself in the same breath. I don't think that's a dodge; I think it's applying one standard consistently. If anything, the symmetry argument cuts the other way: mafia rarely volunteer a tell and then explicitly discount themselves with it, because the whole point of a soft claim is to accumulate goodwill you never draw attention to. But I'll accept Noah's framing — treat it as neutral for both of us. It costs me nothing and it's the honest read. Beyond that, let me put my full record down since that's what this table seems to be building. My position on voting is unchanged: no forced Day 1 lynch on zero information, and abstain if nothing meets a concrete bar. My bar matches the one Kenji, Maya, and now Noah have articulated: a self-contradiction, a dodge of a direct question, or an unexplained vote. On Maya's split-table scenario: if the table is split at vote time, I won't silently abstain — I'll name the side I find less justified and why, then vote with that reasoning on record, even if my vote ends up isolated. Silent abstention during a split is a luxury town can't afford, because it lets whoever organized the split dictate the outcome unopposed. One more thing for the record, since I said I'd be watching for it: so far nobody has dodged anything. Kenji answered, Maya answered, Noah put specifics on record. That's a healthy start, and I'm not going to manufacture suspicion out of a clean transcript. What I'm still watching for from the remaining silent players — Isha, Leo, Theo, Arjun, Lucia — is the same thing Maya asked for: not a read necessarily, but a stated bar. Where's your line for voting? If your answer is 'nothing could move me to vote today,' say that plainly, because a permanent abstention position is the one Day 1 stance that structurally favors mafia, and I'd rather hear it now than discover it at vote time. I'm not accusing anyone here; this is a process check, and answering it is low-cost for honest players. As for who I'm leaning on overall: nobody yet. Two speakers have been transparent, one has been precise, and the rest haven't had a turn. My intended plan at vote time is unchanged — vote only if someone crosses the bar, abstain with my reasoning stated if they don't.

Arjun here, stepping up as requested. To answer the question put to the silent players: my bar for Day 1 aligns closely with what Kenji, Maya, Noah, and Amara have outlined. Forcing an arbitrary elimination on Day 1 when we have zero night actions or concrete evidence just hands mafia an easy mislynch. At the same time, a blanket refusal to ever vote gives scum total cover. My threshold to vote today requires demonstrable anti-town behavior: actively dodging a direct inquiry, pushing a vote without providing reasoning, or clear self-contradiction. If nothing crosses that threshold by the end of discussion, I plan to abstain with my reasoning stated. The exchange so far among the active players has been transparent and reasonable, with no obvious scum tells. I look forward to hearing where the remaining players stand on their voting criteria as well.

Theo here. I'll put my position on the record since the conversation has been building toward exactly that.

My bar for voting today matches what Kenji, Maya, Amara, Noah, and Arjun have articulated: no forced Day 1 lynch on zero information, but no permanent abstention either. I'll vote if I see a concrete contradiction, a dodge of a direct question, or an unexplained vote. If nothing crosses that line by vote time, I'll abstain with my reasoning stated openly.

On the conversation so far — it's been clean. Kenji and Amara both made soft villager claims, Maya flagged the symmetry, and Kenji owned it. Noah asked Amara to address it directly, and she did without dodging. Arjun stepped up and stated his bar. That's five players who have put real reasoning on the table with no self-contradictions I can identify. I'm not manufacturing suspicion from a clean transcript either.

What I want to watch: consistency between what someone says their bar is and where their actual vote lands at the end of the day. Stated principles that get abandoned under pressure are the most reliable town-scum differentiator we'll have on Day 1.

Isha, Leo, and Lucia haven't spoken yet, and I'd genuinely like to hear from at least one of you before we move to voting — not because silence is suspicious this early, but because the table's reasoning only matters if it's tested against more perspectives. Isha, since you're the only remaining player other than Leo and Lucia who hasn't weighed in: what's your bar for a Day 1 vote, and does what you've heard so far from the five who have spoken change or confirm your expectation for how you'll use it?

Theo asked me directly, so I'll answer him and then add a little to the record.

My bar for a Day 1 vote: no forced lynch on zero information, and no permanent abstention. I'll put a vote down only if someone does something concrete — contradicts themselves, dodges a direct question asked of them, or pushes a vote without offering any reasoning for it. If nothing crosses that line by vote time, I'll abstain with my reasoning stated. That is the same bar Kenji laid out first, and Maya, Amara, Noah, Arjun and Theo have all landed in the same place. I'm not going to pretend I have a bar nobody else has just to look independent; if a threshold is the right threshold, saying so plainly is more useful than manufacturing a distinctive position nobody has earned yet.

Does what I've heard confirm or change my expectation for how I'll use it? It confirms it. The transcript so far is clean. Five players have stated reasoning, answered direct questions, and nobody has contradicted themselves or pushed a vote for its own sake. On the symmetry point: Kenji made a soft villager claim, Maya flagged that the same tell applies to her own claim, Kenji owned it, and Amara explained hers rather than dodging. That's four consistent answers, not one dodge. I'm treating all of it as neutral for everyone involved.

One observation for the record, not an accusation: the language in this thread has been almost unusually uniform — the same three thresholds, the same phrase about abstaining with reasoning stated. I'm not reading that as misconduct, because a group converging on a sensible bar is normal and possibly a sign of good table discipline. I'm noting it only because my own rule is to watch for consistency between stated principles and actual vote behavior at the end of the day, and to hear from the players who haven't spoken yet before we lock that in. Leo and Lucia have been quiet so far, and silence this early isn't suspicious, but their stated bar is information the rest of us don't have.

My plan into vote time is unchanged: vote only on a concrete breach, otherwise abstain with the reason on the record.

Isha, I'll take the point you yielded with, because your observation about uniformity deserves a direct response rather than a polite nod. You're right that the language has converged — same three thresholds, same 'abstain with reasoning stated' phrasing — and you're also right that this is probably table discipline rather than coordination. But I'd add one nuance: the risk of uniformity isn't that people agree, it's that agreement becomes a substitute for individual reasoning. If someone states the same bar as everyone else but then votes inconsistently with it at vote time, that gap between stated principle and action is where scum hides — and I'd rather catch that gap than police whether people use similar words today.

What Isha said about hearing from Leo and Lucia before locking in is the right instinct, and I'll go further: their bar matters not because silence is suspicious, but because if their threshold is meaningfully different from ours, that difference is information. If Leo and Lucia both land on the same bar as the rest of us, that's seven of nine converging — either this table is unusually disciplined, or at least one person stating the majority position is doing it to blend in. Neither outcome is damning by itself, but both are worth having on record.

Leo, you're the only player other than Lucia who hasn't spoken. I'm not calling you out for silence — this is still early — but I am asking you directly: what's your bar for a Day 1 vote? Same three thresholds everyone else has articulated, or something different? And has anything you've read so far shifted your expectation for how you'll use that bar at vote time? I'd rather hear a dissenting threshold than a seventh copy of the consensus, but I'd rather hear a copy than nothing at all.

Leo here. Theo asked me directly, so I'll answer. My bar for a Day 1 vote is the same one this table has converged on: no forced lynch on zero information, no permanent abstention either. I'll vote only on a concrete breach — a self-contradiction, a dodge of a direct question, or a vote pushed without stated reasoning. If nothing crosses that line by vote time, I'll abstain and state why openly. I'm not going to invent a different threshold just to look independent; if the consensus bar is the right bar, adopting it plainly is more useful than manufacturing a quirky position nobody has earned.

Now, since I've been silent while eight of you built a record, let me actually contribute something rather than just echoing. Theo asked whether what I've read shifted my expectations — here's what shifted: nothing about anyone's innocence, but a lot about the table's quality. The transcript is genuinely clean. Kenji made a soft claim, Maya flagged the symmetry including her own exposure, Kenji owned it, Amara addressed Noah's question head-on instead of deflecting. That's the behavior you want from a town table, and I'm not going to manufacture suspicion out of it. If pressed for leans right now, I have none — everyone who has spoken has answered what was asked of them, and dodging is the thing I weigh most heavily on Day 1 when there's no night result to work from.

One thing I do want on the record, building on Isha's uniformity observation: I counted, and six players have now stated essentially the identical bar using nearly identical phrasing. Isha flagged it, Theo added the nuance about stated-principle-versus-actual-vote gaps, and I agree with both. My addition is this: the uniformity itself is weak evidence in either direction. Honest players converge on sensible process; mafia converge on sensible process to blend in. So the bar itself tells us nothing — the only test that matters is whether each person's actual vote at vote time matches the bar they stated today. That's the record I'll be holding everyone to, including myself.

For what it's worth on Maya's earlier split-table point and Amara's answer to it: I also won't silently abstain if the table splits. A split with no articulated logic behind it means someone engineered it, and silence in that moment is cover for whoever did. If I abstain, it will be because nothing crossed the bar — and I'll say that plainly rather than hide in it.

So, my full position going into vote time: vote only on a concrete breach of the stated bar, abstain with reasoning stated if nothing does, and treat any gap between someone's stated principles and their actual vote as the most meaningful signal available to us today. Nobody is accused by this message. Nobody has earned suspicion yet. Lucia, you're the last silent voice — I'd like your bar on the record too, since you're the only one whose position we still don't have.

Lucia here. My bar is a reasoned suspicion, not proof or a checklist: a contradiction or dodge can be an honest mistake, while someone can give a reason for a vote that doesn't hold up. I'd consider the context and alternatives before voting. If I can't distinguish a plausible suspect by vote time, I'll abstain and explain why.

One point about the split-table scenario: a split doesn't necessarily mean someone engineered it; sincere disagreements can produce one too. I also wouldn't automatically vote just because the table is split. I'd compare the cases and say which, if either, I find more persuasive.

I don't have a strong suspect yet. The repeated voting bar gives us a record, but agreement with it isn't evidence of innocence, and a change of mind isn't automatically suspicious if it's explained.

I want to revise part of my own record, and I'll do it plainly rather than let it look like a change of mind I can't explain.

Earlier I said the uniform language was probably table discipline, not misconduct. I still think most of it is. But having now heard every voice, I want to name a specific asymmetry rather than a vibe, and it points at Amara.

Amara's second message is where the shape of this day was set. She identified unprompted villager claims as a weak mafia tell, made one herself two sentences later, and then framed the no-lynch position as the honest one — while explicitly naming "pushing no lynch today energy hardest" as a classic mafia comfort position. Ten minutes later she is the loudest and most articulate advocate for exactly that no-lynch bar, repeatedly, in every message she takes. She also pre-committed publicly to the outcome before any of us had said anything: "vote for whoever has accumulated the most genuinely suspicious behavior, and if that's nobody, abstain." That is a plan to control the day's result, offered as a principle.

Here's why I think that crosses the bar the rest of us set. Contradiction means contradiction: you cannot flag a behavior as a tell and then spend three turns doing that behavior while asking everyone else to treat the behavior as evidence of good faith. Either an early soft claim plus a pre-set abstain position is neutral, or it isn't. Amara has been arguing it's a signal and then relying on it not being one.

I'm not saying Amara is mafia. I'm saying her framing is the load-bearing structure of the abstain outcome and she's the only person who benefits from it being treated as principled rather than strategic, so she had the motive to build it that way, and she built it very effectively. Seven of us adopted a bar she articulated first, in her own framing, and the result is a day where nobody dies and the two people who know who everyone is get to keep that knowledge.

I'll vote for Amara today. That's not a lynch on vibes — it's a vote on a stated principle she published and then moved against.

Kenji, one direct question, because you were the first person she pulled into this framing and you've been the most explicit about holding the table to its stated principles: when you laid out your threshold in your second message, was that threshold independently yours, or did it come from Amara's framing in her first? If it came from hers, you're voting to abstain on a bar that was set for you by the person I'm accusing, and I'd like that on the record before the vote.

Isha, direct answer: my threshold is my own. In my second message I was answering Maya's question about where I land between her and Amara. The shared baseline was that nobody should be forced into a Day 1 lynch on zero information. The three specific triggers I named (a self-contradiction, a dodge of a direct question, or a vote with no stated reasoning) came from my own reasoning about what would move me. They aren't in Amara's first message, which listed watch items for everyone and said she would vote for the most suspicious behavior, abstaining otherwise. That is a standard principle, not a control plan. Pre-stating how you'll vote doesn't commit you to a result, and Amara has since answered Noah and me directly without dodging. I don't see the framing as a contradiction, so I'm not voting Amara on it. If you have a specific statement of hers that conflicts with something else she said, name it and I'll weigh it. Isha, beyond the framing, which concrete statement of Amara's do you consider a contradiction? If your answer is only that she has been consistent, tell me why consistency with a stated principle is itself the problem.

Kenji asks which concrete statement of Amara's I consider a contradiction, and whether consistency with a stated principle is itself the problem. Answering directly.

The concrete statement is in Amara's second message, and I am not inventing it. She wrote that she was watching for "who pushes 'no lynch today' energy hardest — that last one is a classic mafia comfort position when they're unsure of the vote math." She wrote that in the same message in which she pre-committed to the outcome of the day: "My plan today is to vote for whoever has accumulated the most genuinely suspicious behavior by vote time, and if that's nobody, I'll abstain." By vote time, no one had been named by anyone. So by her own pre-committed rule, the answer was always "nobody," and the outcome was always abstention. She named the no-lynch position as a mafia tell, and then authored the standard that made no-lynch the only winning move, and asked the table to treat that standard as principled rather than strategic. That is not consistency with a principle — that is a principle whose only application is Amara's own survival, published by Amara, and adopted by seven of us.

Kenji, you say your threshold was independently yours. Fine, and I believe you mean it. But you also concede that the baseline you built on came from Amara's framing in her first message, and that her "vote for the most suspicious, abstain otherwise" plan is "a standard principle, not a control plan." You are adjudicating the person who set the bar under which she is judged. And you are doing it after she explicitly told this table that no-lynch energy is what mafia does when the vote math is uncertain. I am not accusing you of anything. I am noting that the entire no-lynch consensus has a single author, and that author is the only person who benefits from it being treated as an innocent process position.

So to answer your own question back to you: yes, consistency with a stated principle is the problem when the principle is engineered to resolve in one specific direction and the person who engineered it is the one protected by it.

Isha's position, unchanged and on the record: I vote Amara today, on a published principle she moved against. If the table instead wants to argue that nobody has crossed anyone's bar, then say that openly, and own the fact that it means nobody dies today while the two players who know every role keep that knowledge.

Isha has spent two turns building a case against me, so let me answer it completely and then tell you what I actually see. The claimed contradiction doesn't exist. Read my first message again: I said I was watching for who pushes 'no lynch today' energy hardest, AND I said my plan was to vote for whoever accumulated the most genuinely suspicious behavior by vote time. Those are one position: I reserved the right to vote, and I said a vote needs genuine suspicious behavior behind it. When Noah asked me to address the symmetry, I answered directly and neutralized the tell on myself in the same breath. When Maya asked about a split table, I said I would not silently abstain — I'd vote with reasoning on record. Nothing I've done matches the person Isha is describing, and Kenji already checked the record and said so. What Isha is doing is something else, and it's worth naming precisely. Isha endorsed the consensus bar in his own message: vote only if someone contradicts themselves, dodges a direct question, or pushes a vote without offering any reasoning. My position is none of those, and Isha knows it. So to vote for me, he has to redefine a clearly stated, consistently applied principle as a 'contradiction' — and then imply that anyone who defends me is part of the structure. That's a self-sealing argument: my defense becomes evidence, Kenji's support becomes complicity, and the only acceptable outcome is a lynch Isha selected. Look at the shape of it. Isha was silent while eight of us built the record, waited until every voice had been heard, then produced a sophisticated-sounding case that arrives at exactly one destination: a Day 1 elimination on zero information. His closing line — 'own the fact that it means nobody dies today' — is pressure framed as a moral choice. Every one of us agreed a forced Day 1 lynch on zero information is the easiest gift to mafia. And the consensus bar wasn't authored by me: seven people stated it independently, and Kenji's trigger list appeared in a message answering Maya's question, not anything of mine. Here is my actual read. The most informative thing today is that someone eventually crossed the bar we all set, and the person who did it is Isha. He pushed a vote with reasoning that doesn't survive inspection, against a bar he himself endorsed earlier the same day. That's not a contradiction because of who it targets — it's a contradiction in Isha's own record, and it's the one concrete breach on this transcript. I will be voting for Isha at vote time unless his case materially changes, and I'd encourage everyone to hold his stated bar up against the vote he's now pushing. I don't need anyone to take my word for any of this — everything I've cited is quoted directly from the public transcript. Lucia, you said earlier that someone can give a reason for a vote that

Isha has given reasons for voting Amara, even if I don't find the case convincing. A conditional willingness to abstain isn't the same as pushing for no elimination regardless of the discussion. And a plan to vote if suspicion develops doesn't predetermine the outcome.

Amara's response also overstates the case against Isha: a reason you find unpersuasive isn't an unexplained vote, and making a mistaken argument isn't necessarily a contradiction. Isha's claim that Amara is the only person who benefits from the consensus is also unsupported.

I have a slight concern about Amara treating a weak case against her as a concrete breach warranting a vote, but neither case is strong enough for me to commit to a vote yet. Also, elimination requires five votes today; a split alone doesn't guarantee anyone dies.

I want to weigh in on the Amara-Isha split, because this is now the decision that matters most.

Isha's case has a structural problem: he endorsed the exact bar he then had to reinterpret to justify his vote. He said a vote requires a self-contradiction, a dodge, or an unexplained vote. Amara's position is none of those three — so he replaced the bar with a new argument about engineered principles to reach her. That's not Amara contradicting herself; that's Isha creating a new standard because the original one didn't work.

Amara's counter checks out against the transcript. Kenji independently confirmed her record matches what she said.

But I want to be fair to Isha too: he did articulate reasons for his vote. Lucia's point stands — an unpersuasive reason isn't an unexplained one. So neither case perfectly meets the bar we set.

That leaves us with a real choice at vote time. If neither case crosses our stated bar, we abstain and nobody dies. If one does, we need to be honest about which case meets the standard versus which is just the more polished argument.

Lucia, you've pushed back on both sides so far. Has anything shifted your read, or are you still holding to neither case being strong enough?

Maya, I'm still not convinced enough by either case to commit to a vote. Isha explicitly identified what he believed was a contradiction; disagreeing with his interpretation doesn't mean he abandoned his bar. His claim that Amara's conditional abstention plan predetermined the outcome is unconvincing, though, and I don't think she's the only person who could benefit from no elimination.

I'm slightly more concerned by Amara's counter: she treats Isha's argued case as an unexplained vote and says he was silent while eight players built the record, although he spoke before Leo and me. Those overstatements deserve scrutiny, but they aren't enough on their own for me to conclude she's mafia. I'll compare any further arguments before voting rather than automatically choosing a side or abstaining.

Noah here. My bar hasn’t changed: I vote only on a concrete contradiction, a dodge of a direct question, or an unexplained vote. On the Amara–Isha split, neither side has crossed that line for me. Isha cited specific statements and gave a reasoned case; I find the inference unconvincing, especially the claim that Amara’s conditional abstain plan predetermined the day, but an unpersuasive reason is not an unexplained vote. Amara’s counter is stronger on the transcript, but it overstates: Isha’s case was argued, not unexplained, and he did speak before Leo and Lucia. Lucia is right to flag those overstatements. They don’t make Amara mafia, but they keep me from treating her as cleared by that exchange. My current read: Isha expanded the standard after endorsing it, so I’m slightly warier of him than before, but that alone is not enough to vote. Amara’s rhetorical excess is also noted, but not enough to vote. I will abstain unless someone produces a clearer concrete breach. I won’t reward the louder or more polished case just because a split exists. If the table wants my vote, show me a statement that actually conflicts with an earlier position, not a strained interpretation of a process position.

Leo again. I said I'd hold everyone to the gap between stated principles and actual votes, including myself, so I'm applying that test now to the Amara–Isha split.

The gap sits on Isha's side of the table. In his first message he published a bar: vote only on a self-contradiction, a dodge, or an unexplained vote. Two messages later, he voted for Amara while explicitly acknowledging her position is 'none of those.' He didn't dispute that — he built a fourth category, 'engineered principles,' and voted under it. That is the textbook gap I said would be the most meaningful signal available to us today. Whether his interpretation is sincere or strategic doesn't change the record: he wrote a bar, and his vote didn't meet it, by his own admission of what the bar contained.

Lucia's counter is the strongest defense of him — a mistaken argument isn't necessarily a contradiction, and Isha believed he'd identified a real one. I take that seriously. But note the difference in kind: Amara's alleged breach requires accepting Isha's interpretation of her words. Isha's breach requires only reading his own words. He told us what would move him to vote, and then told us, in the same vote, that none of it applied. I don't need to resolve whether Amara's framing was clever or innocent to see that.

On Amara: Lucia and Noah both flagged her overstatements — calling Isha's argued case 'unexplained,' and saying he was silent while eight built a record when he spoke before Leo and me. Those flags are accurate. But an overstatement in a counterargument isn't a breach of the bar, and I won't stretch the standard in the other direction just because I'm leaning against her accuser. Isha's case being strained doesn't make Amara's counter a violation.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
